What it means: The City Council held a hearing on Docket 0773 to review Boston's curbside food waste diversion program and waste management strategies [02:33, 03:57]. City officials explained that food waste accounts for roughly one-third of collected residential waste [13:11] and announced a transition from weekly to biweekly collection starting in October [18:20, 19:50]. This operational change is estimated to save around $7,000 [19:31] while enabling the city to absorb waitlisted households into the active pickup system [18:42, 31:48]. Officials also detailed broader waste diversion challenges, including regional composting capacity constraints and the use of anaerobic digestion for processed organic material [16:57, 27:12, 35:07].

Who moved it: The hearing was sponsored by Councilor Sharon Durkan [02:51] and co-sponsored by Councilor Cledus Bartlett [03:47, 03:50], with Councilor Gallardo Zapata also recognized for supporting the effort [06:01]. The discussion included testimony from Chief of Streets Chris Osgoode [07:56], Chief Brian Swett [04:07, 10:27], and Waste Policy and Planning official Avantika Mathur [04:16, 10:32], alongside questions from attending council members [05:56, 28:28, 29:05].

What to watch: The city plans to roll out the new biweekly schedule in October and begin processing roughly 1,600 waitlisted households into the service [19:50, 31:48, 48:00]. Councilors requested targeted community outreach and zoomed-in meetings on pest control and accessibility for specific neighborhoods like Chinatown and Mattapan [37:15, 109:27, 112:40]. Officials noted they will continue evaluating regional infrastructure needs as state organic waste recovery requirements evolve toward 2028 [116:29, 117:07]. The transcript does not record any formal votes taken during this hearing [135:02, 135:25].

summary: The City Services Committee met on September 18, 2026, to review Boston's curbside food waste collection program and Project Oscar community drop-off locations [02:38], [04:52]. Officials discussed plans to switch curbside compost collection from weekly to biweekly pickups beginning October 5th [18:25], [19:54], [20:01]. City staff explained that moving to biweekly service will allow the city to clear its 1,600-household waitlist [18:34], expand enrollment across neighborhoods [18:43], and lower vehicle emissions by reducing truck routes [30:20]. The committee and panelists also addressed waste processing through anaerobic digestion [16:57], [35:27], pest control considerations [08:40], access to drop-off bins [49:12], and constituent education and outreach [09:14], [33:45].
